:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,2)$ and $(-2,2),$ traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/7c/7ca4b6fe3a5a16c4004c75b0e4524cc3b42550cb2413d5b8e1c21a1d53cee902.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3})dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{8{y}^{3}}{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{[{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot {2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$ where $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡y,{x}^{2}-2y⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the square $0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi ,$ traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/4f/4f75ee554c61dc799273c2c731d608766d27987937d0058df6ee1e0290d8b060.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi \}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{[2xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi }\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\pi x+2)\,dx \\  & ={[\pi {x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & ={\pi }^{3}+2\pi  \\  & =\pi ({\pi }^{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$ where $F(x,y)=(3xy-1)\,i+(3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y})\,j$ and $C$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/5f/5f34ac74599937e0ae181126ff9a3da5b29dfe213614a1f23ca10c7062f22f7d.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(3xy-1)\,dx+(3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=3xy-1$ and $Q(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =6x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 2x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(3xy-1)\,dx+(3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(6x-3x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2x}3x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3x[y]_{{x}^{2}}^{2x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3x(2x-{x}^{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{x}^{2}-3{x}^{3})\,dx \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2(2)^{3}-\frac{3(2)^{4}}{4} \\  & =16-12 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/57/574172dda3031b9bb44dbcfb46265453ae543a75bccf8db24e93625e7154bba9.png)

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{y}+{x}^{2})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}-{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{y}+{x}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[2xy+{y}^{2}]}_{-1}^{1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2x(1)+(1)^{2}-2x(-1)-(-1)^{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}4x\,dx \\  & =2{[{x}^{2}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2[(1)^{2}-(-1)^{2}] \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/e7/e788bbcbda4cc715c6989b7de9d08d60e3b0d178eeb9432a342a4c86c4c01b86.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=2y-x$ and $Q(x,y)=5x-y.$ Therefore,

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y-x)\,dx+(5x-y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}-x}^{x}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}[y]_{{x}^{2}-x}^{x}\,dx \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\,dx \\  & =3{[{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3(4-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}2xy\,dx+{y}^{2}\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}$ and $y=\sqrt{3x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/eb/eb0b120cc4d63c8dab18c8acb37f5835e99db746584262f6bb33e8ca99b6a16d.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=2xy$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\le y\le \sqrt{3x}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}2xy\,dx+{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(0-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{{x}^{2}/3}^{\sqrt{3x}}(-2x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2x)[y]_{{x}^{2}/3}^{\sqrt{3x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2x)(\sqrt{3x}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{3}{x}^{3/2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})dx \\  & =-2{[\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{3x}}{5}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{12}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-2(\frac{2(3)^{2}\sqrt{3(3)}}{5}-\frac{(3)^{4}}{12}) \\  & =-2(\frac{54}{5}-\frac{27}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{81}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/fa/fafd281fc63fb276c9759fd84f722096d494aa3e3fe9441f43aa6ecd1f9dfda9.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(2x+{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2x+{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}/3}(2x-2y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2xy-{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{{x}^{2}/3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{9})dx \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{4}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{45}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{(3)^{4}}{6}-\frac{(3)^{5}}{45} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-\frac{27}{5} \\  & =\frac{81}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

$$ where $C$ is the boundary of the trapezoid with vertices at $(0,1),$ $(0,-5),$ $(4,-1)$ and $(4,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/ac/acd7ae0cc90007b9f710f242ab1f0498b2439cdbb8951df388b9d8d0588d553f.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(2x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dx+(x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=2x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =1+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 4,\,x-5\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dx+(x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{x-5}^{1}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[y]_{x-5}^{1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(6-x)\,dx \\  & ={[6x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =24-\frac{16}{2} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

$$ where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(1,2)$ and $(0,2),$ traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/a8/a87f696b1eb42588ab69800b72d821bf47b35676fc19dcd4fe2927bbf36ba3f8.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= 4x^2y$ and $Q(x,y)= 2y^2.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 1,\, 2x \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}4{x}^{2}y\,dx+2{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(0-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{2}(-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[y]_{2x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(2-2x)\,dx \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-x)\,dx \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}\,dx \\  & =-8{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{1}{12} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate

$$
\oint_C (2y-x)\,dx+(5x+y)\,dy,
$$

where $C$ is the boundary of the rectangle $-1\le x\le3$, $0\le y\le2$, traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

The enclosed region $D$ and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/39/3954846460076fa1ef1e5826d32bde9145e7350cb2324072b001d8c6ff41cc14.png)

Here $P=2y-x$ and $Q=5x+y$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=2,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=5,\\
Q_x-P_y&=3.\end{aligned}
$$

The bounds of $D$ are $-1\le x\le3$ and $0\le y\le2$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C (2y-x)\,dx+(5x+y)\,dy
&=\int_{-1}^{3}\int_0^2 3\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_{-1}^{3}[3y]_0^2\,dx\\
&=\int_{-1}^{3}6\,dx\\
&=[6x]_{-1}^{3}\\
&=18-(-6)\\
&=24.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, the constant curl $3$ is multiplied by the rectangle's area $(3-(-1))(2-0)=8$.

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate

$$
\oint_C xy\,dx+(x^2+y^2)\,dy,
$$

where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,2)$ and $(0,2)$, traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

The enclosed region $D$ and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/a8/a87f696b1eb42588ab69800b72d821bf47b35676fc19dcd4fe2927bbf36ba3f8.png)

Here $P=xy$ and $Q=x^2+y^2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2x,\\
Q_x-P_y&=x.\end{aligned}
$$

The sloping side through $(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$ is $y=2x$. Vertical slices run from $y=2x$ to $y=2$, with $0\le x\le1$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C xy\,dx+(x^2+y^2)\,dy
&=\int_0^1\int_{2x}^{2}x\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1[xy]_{2x}^{2}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1(2x-2x^2)\,dx\\
&=\left[x^2-\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\
&=1-\frac23=\frac13.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r,
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle xy+y^2,\,2x^2+e^y\rangle$ and $C$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=x^2$ and $y=2x$, traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

The enclosed region $D$ and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/5f/5f34ac74599937e0ae181126ff9a3da5b29dfe213614a1f23ca10c7062f22f7d.png)

Writing the vector line integral in differential form gives

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\oint_C(xy+y^2)\,dx+(2x^2+e^y)\,dy.
$$

Here $P=xy+y^2$ and $Q=2x^2+e^y$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=x+2y,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=4x,\\
Q_x-P_y&=3x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersections satisfy $x^2=2x$, so $x(x-2)=0$ and $x=0,2$. On $0\le x\le2$, the parabola $y=x^2$ is below the line $y=2x$. Thus $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le2,\ x^2\le y\le2x\}$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
&=\int_0^2\int_{x^2}^{2x}(3x-2y)\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^2[3xy-y^2]_{x^2}^{2x}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^2\bigl((6x^2-4x^2)-(3x^3-x^4)\bigr)\,dx\\
&=\int_0^2(x^4-3x^3+2x^2)\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac{x^5}{5}-\frac{3x^4}{4}+\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^2\\
&=\frac{32}{5}-12+\frac{16}{3}=-\frac{4}{15}.
\end{aligned}
$$
